title: A measurement, quantitative identification and estimation method(QINRW) of non-rainfall water component by lysimeter
author: Zhang, Wang, et al.
materials: Thus far, each component of NRW is determined.

steps.title: Set up observation instruments
steps.instruction: Install all required sensors and the lysimeter according to the specifications and connect them to data loggers.

substeps.instruction: Mount HMP45D humidity‑and‑temperature probes at heights 1 m, 2 m, 4 m, 10 m and 16 m; set sampling interval to every 10 min.
Place the surface temperature sensor (model 109, Campbell Scientific, USA) at 0 cm depth; set sampling interval to every 10 min.
Install dust collectors (JJ1000 electronic balance + dust‑full jar, accuracy 0.01 g, range 0‑1000 g) on the ground to collect dust on rainless days.

Set up the large LG‑I lysimeter (diameter 2.25 m, effective area 4.0 m², depth 2.65 m) equipped with a high‑resolution weighing system (accuracy 0.03 mm, sensitivity 0.01 mm); configure it to record weight every hour.
Connect a rain gauge (accuracy ±2.5 %) for precipitation measurement and verify all data collectors and signal sensors are powered and communicating.

steps.title: Collect raw data
steps.instruction: Record all meteorological, dust, and lysimeter measurements continuously during the monitoring period.

substeps.instruction: Log hourly lysimeter weight values.
Log wind, temperature and humidity at the five heights every 10 min.
Log surface temperature every 10 min.
Weigh dust collected each rainless day with the electronic balance.
Record precipitation amounts from the rain gauge.

steps.title: Pre‑process lysimeter data
steps.instruction: Clean the raw lysimeter time series to remove periods that could bias the water‑balance calculation.

substeps.instruction: Delete all data points that fall within rainfall, snowfall or sand‑storm periods.
Visually inspect the remaining series and discard obvious outliers from unreliable periods.
Apply a threshold filter: discard any hourly change greater than 0.08 mm h⁻¹ (Δw > 0.08 mm/h).
For isolated missing values (a single hour or two consecutive hours), fill by linear‑trend interpolation using the two adjacent valid points.
Leave long‑term gaps unfilled (no imputation).

steps.title: Calculate hourly weight change
steps.instruction: Determine the mass variation for each hour to identify possible water gain.

substeps.instruction: For each hour i, compute Δw = w_i – w_{i‑1} (kg). Positive Δw indicates a weight increase.

steps.title: Compute dew‑point temperature
steps.instruction: Derive Td from the saturated vapor pressure using the prescribed formula.

substeps.instruction: Calculate saturated vapor pressure e_w (from measured temperature and relative humidity).
Note: the formula is valid for –45 °C ≤ Td ≤ +60 °C with an uncertainty of ±0.04 °C.

steps.title: Identify NRW and its components
steps.instruction: Use a five‑step decision tree to classify any positive Δw as a specific non‑rainfall water component.

substeps.instruction: a) If Δw ≤ 0, assume no NRW; if Δw > 0, proceed to step b.
b) Check precipitation data for the same hour: if precipitation occurred, attribute Δw to rain and stop; if not, continue.
c) Check dust‑collector data for the same hour: if dust mass increased, attribute Δw to dry deposition and stop; if not, continue.
d) Examine relative humidity (RH): if RH = 100 %, classify the remaining NRW as fog; otherwise continue to step e.
e) Compare surface temperature (Ts) with dew‑point temperature (Td): if Ts < Td, classify as dew; if Ts ≥ Td, classify as water‑vapor adsorption (WVA).

steps.title: Aggregate component amounts
steps.instruction: Sum the identified dew, fog and WVA values over the desired analysis periods.

substeps.instruction: Group the classified NRW values into 10‑day intervals (or any other chosen period).
Calculate total millimetres of dew, fog and WVA for each interval.

steps.title: Validate and interpret results
steps.instruction: Compare the seasonal pattern of the calculated NRW with expected trends and literature.

substeps.instruction: Check that autumn shows higher NRW totals than summer, consistent with higher evapotranspiration in summer.
Document any discrepancies for further investigation.
